thread.title: Stocks Slide as Apple Raises Concern on Two Fronts

title: Stocks Slide as Apple Raises Concern on Two Fronts
text:
Stocks Slide as Apple Raises Concern on Two Fronts By Nov. 12, 2018 12:33 p.m. ET Order Reprints Illustration by Michael Haddad Text size
Manic Monday. Stocks were lower to start the week, as tech remains a focal point for investors, although worries about global growth persist. In today’s Midday Movers, we…
…talk about tech’s tumble;
…see why some analysts are still hopeful;
…and turn to the tao of Larry David.
Apple Anxiety
All three major indexes were in the red early Monday, although tech is bearing the brunt of the pain.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.6% while the S&P 500 was off 1.4% and the Nasdaq Composite had fallen 2.2%.
Apple (ticker: AAPL) is causing concern due to reports that it slashed its iPhone production orders , while economic slowdowns in emerging markets are also a worry for the company. That rolls the markets’ two biggest sources of recent (non-election) anxiety—slowing global growth and shakiness in the FAANG stocks—into one.
Yet BlackRock’s Richard Turnill argues that there are still reasons for optimism about technology stocks, especially Chinese tech, which has also been hurt by tariff worries and regulatory changes, two factors that have brought down earnings estimates. He notes that strong consumer demand should lead a rebound in 2019, while Chinese tech stocks have a more domestic bent. That’s good news, he says, given the growth of the Chinese middle class and that nation’s increased allocation of capital to its “innovation priorities.” Ultimately, he writes, the long-term potential of Chinese tech is being obscured by the trade war.
“We advocate digging deeper than the index-dominating mega-cap names in China to uncover opportunities in smaller software and services firms,” he writes. “In the U.S., we favor software as a service (SaaS) firms, as companies large and small move their systems to the cloud. Valuation multiples in the U.S. tech sector have risen in the post-crisis period but are now in line with their five-year historical average, and they do not look particularly extended over a longer horizon.”
More optimism in tech would go a long way toward soothing equity markets. The sector is the biggest market component in both the U.S. and China.
Of course, while today’s move is painful, and follows Friday’s lackluster performance, last week was still a good one for stocks overall. It’s a sign that equities have been recovering their footing after a rough October, now that elections are behind us. Newsletter Sign-up
Piper Jaffray’s Crain Johnson writes that he remains “encouraged by the market’s recovery off the October lows. Momentum and market breadth are also moving in the right direction,” leading him to believe that despite some head winds, it still makes sense to add exposure to U.S. stocks.
While the big bounce that followed the midterm elections was brief, HSBC ’s Ben Laidler echoes the sentiment that after a frightful October, stocks’ risk-reward profile has improved. “Investor sentiment remains negative—a contrarian positive—whilst global valuations have derated sharply and are now below [the] long-term average,” he writes. “Earnings per share expectations remain in double-digit territory. We believe margins are broadly resilient to wage and tariff concerns.”
That may sound like cold comfort today, however, given the market action. While investors may be relieved that the overhang of midterm elections is over, other worries have rushed in to fill the void.
Yes, markets generally rise after midterms, with the S&P 500 up 13.8% on average, in the following six months going back to 1946, writes CFRA’s Sam Stovall. And yes, the index has been up 100% of the time in the year after the election, with an average price increase of 14.5%.However, a split Congress and Republican president result in the lowest average calendar-year price changes in history, he says. “Therefore, even though gridlock may be good, it ain’t great, and investors would be wise to temper their enthusiasm for the year ahead,” Stovall writes.
So curb your enthusiasm, but don’t give up hope that markets can be pretty good .
Midday Movers
American Airlines (AAL) was up 1.3% to $36.71 after Goldman Sachs initiated coverage on the stock with a Buy rating.
Crocs (CROX) rose 2.4% to $25.99 after Susquehanna upgraded it to Neutral from Negative.
Dell Technologies (DVMT) fell down 1.1% to $97.02 after activist investor Carl Icahn urged shareholders to reject Dell’s $109 per-share offer.
General Electric (GE) was down 4.8% to $8.17 after Credit Suisse lowered its target to $10 from $12, among other issues .
Michael Kors (KORS) gained 1% to $48.28 after Argus upgraded it to Hold .
